analysis.one_liner: Repeals EPA incentives that pay oil and gas companies to cut methane leaks, and the methane emissions fee.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote, so the methane incentive program and emissions charge it targeted stayed in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out an EPA program that pays oil and gas companies to find and fix methane leaks, and would repeal the fee Congress created in 2022 that charges large oil and gas facilities for the methane they emit. Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas that drives climate change and often escapes as wasted natural gas from drilling operations. The bill got no action after being referred to committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the bill would mainly benefit oil and gas producers, especially those operating in the Permian Basin of Texas and New Mexico. Ending the incentive program removes the EPA framework rewarding companies for plugging methane leaks, and repealing the methane fee means large emitting facilities would no longer pay for the methane they release. That lowers operating costs for drillers while the public continues to absorb the pollution.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Section 136 of the Clean Air Act, ending the EPA program that gives petroleum and natural gas systems incentives to cut methane and other greenhouse gas emissions.
It also repeals the charge on methane emissions from large oil and gas facilities required to report their emissions to the EPA, removing a fee on polluters.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost: methane is a potent greenhouse gas, so weaker incentives to plug leaks and waste mean more climate pollution and more wasted natural gas that could otherwise be sold, with the public picking up the tab through climate and air-quality harms.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through more methane pollution

drawbacks.text: Eliminating the incentive program removes EPA support for oil and gas companies to capture methane leaks and waste, which the methane fee repeal would otherwise discourage them from doing.
Repealing the methane emissions charge would remove a financial penalty on polluting facilities, weakening the main price signal pushing drillers to fix leaks.
The bill was referred to committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, so it never faced public scrutiny or debate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to oil and gas operators are real but narrow: they avoid the paperwork of a voluntary incentive program and potential emissions charges. The costs fall broadly: slower methane reductions means more waste, more pollution, and likely higher compliance costs down the road if stricter rules come later, plus forfeited public climate gains. The bill does not deliver savings or protections to ordinary people to balance those costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Representative August Pfluger introduced the bill on August 26, 2022, with 21 Republican cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day.
No further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill never reached the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one changed anything: the methane incentive program and emissions charge remained in place, and the oil and gas companies that would have benefited from repeal gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The methane rules stayed; oil companies gained nothing

for.name: August Pfluger
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the methane incentive program and emissions charge.

for.name: 21 House Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors including Arrington, Herrell, Babin, Balderson, Ellzey, Perry, Budd, Taylor, Newhouse, Miller, Hinson, Bice, Roy, Hudson, Harris, Fallon, Mullin, Estes, Jackson, and Biggs

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic-controlled House never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate a program designed to reduce methane waste from oil and gas operations and repeal a fee charged on methane emissions from large facilities, cutting costs for operators in the Permian Basin and elsewhere. The savings would go to companies, not consumers, while the emissions would remain a public cost.
By ending the EPA incentive program that pays companies to find and fix methane leaks, the bill would reduce demand for leak-detection services and equipment.
